title: Corps
excerpt: The corps is usually the oldest student association in a Dutch city, built on old traditions.
example: For generations people at the corps have been drinking in the sociëteit in exactly the same way.
text: A corps runs on tradition. It often has a long hierarchy of smaller groups like disputen and jaarclubs, with its own unwritten rules, called mores. Members are known for their suits, their confidence and their loyalty. The closest thing abroad is an American frat.

title: Couple goals
excerpt: You say couple goals about a couple that is so cute, sweet or strong together that you want the same.
example: "They've come to the reunion together for ten years and they're still in love. Couple goals."
text: Couple goals is a lot like relationship goals. It is just more about the couple themselves and how they treat each other. You see it under photos of couples on social media all the time.

title: Cover charge
excerpt: A cover charge is the entry fee you pay to get into a club, bar or party.
example: "After midnight the cover charge is fifteen euros. So we need to be on time."
text: A cover charge usually only pays for entry, not for drinks. Sometimes you get a drink token with it. People on the guest list often pay less or nothing at all.

title: Cramming
excerpt: Cramming means stuffing as much study material into your head as possible in a very short time, usually right before an exam.
example: "The exam is tomorrow at nine and I just started chapter one. Time for cramming."
text: Cramming sometimes helps you remember something for a day. But a week later it is usually gone again. It often goes hand in hand with an all-nighter. Dutch students call an exam a tenta.

title: Crash out
excerpt: Crash out means someone loses control and completely explodes with anger or frustration.
example: "He lost at beer pong for the third time and totally crashed out."
text: Someone who crashes out reacts on impulse, without thinking. The word blew up on TikTok around 2023. A person who explodes easily is called a crashout. Sometimes crash out also just means falling asleep from exhaustion.

title: Creator economy
excerpt: The creator economy is the world where people earn money with their own online content and audience.
example: "He dropped out to join the creator economy full time."
text: In the creator economy people earn money through sponsorships, subscriptions, merch and ads. Think of streamers, YouTubers, podcasters and influencers. For a lot of young people it is a dream job. But it is far from always stable.

title: Cringe
excerpt: Cringe is something so embarrassing that you feel ashamed for it, even if you didn't do it yourself.
example: "He sang her a song he wrote himself in the middle of the canteen. So cringe."
text: To cringe means to shrink back. That is exactly what you do when someone does something awkward. Old status updates and photos from when you were twelve are often cringe too. The Dutch have a word for an awkward vibe: krokant.

title: Cuffing season
excerpt: Cuffing season is the time in autumn and winter when people suddenly want a steady relationship.
example: "He was single and happy all summer. Now it's November and he has three dates a week. Cuffing season."
text: Cuffing comes from handcuffs: you want to be tied to someone. When it is cold and dark, sitting on the couch together suddenly sounds very appealing. Around spring some of those couples split up again.

title: Cursist
excerpt: Cursist is a teasing word some Dutch university students use for students at a university of applied sciences (hbo).
example: "So are you a cursist or do you actually study?" he joked to his hbo friend.
text: The Netherlands has research universities (wo) and universities of applied sciences (hbo). Some wo students like to tease hbo students by calling them course takers, or cursisten. It is a joke, mostly. Hbo students usually have a few jokes of their own ready.

title: Cursus
excerpt: Cursus (Dutch for course) is a teasing word some Dutch university students use for an hbo programme.
example: "Are you doing a degree or just a cursus?" he asked with a grin.
text: It is said with a light mocking tone. The joke is that an hbo programme would be lighter than a university degree. Like a little course. It is all part of the friendly rivalry between wo and hbo students.

title: Dapri
excerpt: Dapri is short for Datumprikker, the Dutch tool every student group uses to pick a date.
example: "Can someone make a dapri for the borrel next month?" she texted the group.
text: Students use it to find a date that works for their dispuut, house or association. Everyone ticks the days they can make it. In theory that is quick. In practice there is always someone who fills it in three weeks late.

title: Das
excerpt: Das is Dutch student slang for a tie, often worn as part of the dress code of a dispuut.
example: Before the gala he still had to find a decent das.
text: Within an association or dispuut the das is often part of the fixed dress code for borrels and official events. Sometimes even with its own colours. Lose it and you will hear about it.

title: Datediner
excerpt: A datediner is a dinner with a date, often organised by your dispuut, house or association.
example: For the datediner her dispuut had matched her with a fun date.
text: Students often organise a datediner with their jaarclub, student house or association. Don't know anyone to bring? Then they sometimes set you up with someone. Half blind date, half dinner party.

title: Dead
excerpt: You say dead when something is so funny or absurd that you can't stop laughing.
example: He sent a video of his housemate falling asleep in the bar. "I'm dead."
text: Dead is not meant literally, of course. "I'm dead" means you can't stop laughing. Usually with a skull emoji. It is close to LMAO or sending me.

title: Deadline
excerpt: A deadline is the very last moment something has to be handed in or finished.
example: "The deadline is tonight at 23:59 and my group hasn't done anything yet."
text: Student life revolves around deadlines for assignments, essays and sign-ups. Put it off too long and you end up pulling an all-nighter. A missed deadline can cost you points or a resit. Dutch students call a resit a her.

title: Dealbreaker
excerpt: A dealbreaker is something that makes you not want to continue with someone, for example in a relationship.
example: "He never wants kids and I do. That's just a dealbreaker for me."
text: A dealbreaker is a clear line. It is about things that really matter, like values, honesty or plans for the future. That is different from an ick, which is often just a small annoying detail.

title: Deepfake
excerpt: A deepfake is a video, photo or audio made or edited with AI, where someone seems to do or say something that never happened.
example: "That video of the prime minister rapping? That's just a deepfake."
text: Deepfakes look more real every year. Sometimes they are meant as a joke. But they are also used for scams, fake news and unwanted nude images. So always check the source before you share something.

title: Delulu
excerpt: Delulu is short for delusional. You believe in something unrealistic because you really want it to be true.
example: "He looked at me once in the lecture hall. I think he wants to marry me." "You're so delulu."
text: Delulu started in fan culture, with fans who thought their idol would pick them. Now it is also about dating, your career or your grades. People often say it about themselves. Famous motto: delulu is the solulu.

title: Designated driver
excerpt: The designated driver is the person in the group who doesn't drink, so they can drive everyone home safely.
example: "Who's the designated driver tonight?" Everyone looked at Lisa.
text: In the Netherlands the designated driver is called the BOB, after a famous road safety campaign. It is best to decide beforehand. That way there is a clear plan to get home safely. In English it is often shortened to DD.

title: Despo
excerpt: Despo is Dutch slang for Desperados, the beer with a tequila flavour.
example: There was only one bottle of despo left in the fridge from the last borrel.
text: It stands out from regular lager because of the hint of tequila. That makes it a party favourite. If someone shows up with a crate of despo, you know what kind of night it is going to be.

title: Deur verdienen
excerpt: Deur verdienen (earning your door) is a tradition in some Dutch student houses where a new housemate has to earn their bedroom door.
example: Without a door on his room, he really had to do his best the first few weeks to earn it.
text: With this tradition a new housemate starts without a door on their room. It only goes back on once they meet a certain condition the house came up with. Not every student house does this. But those that do never forget it.

title: Dibs
excerpt: Calling dibs means claiming something or a spot before anyone else can take it.
example: "Dibs on the couch!" she shouted, just a little faster than her housemate.
text: Call dibs first and that spot or thing is yours. It is like calling shotgun for the front seat, but for anything. In a student house it is used for the last slice of pizza, the good chair and the shower in the morning.

title: Dichtgetikt
excerpt: Dichtgetikt is what you are when you can only talk about your student association and its jargon.
example: At family parties he was so dichtgetikt by now that nobody could follow him anymore.
text: Someone who is dichtgetikt only talks about student life, their association and everything around it. Full of words outsiders don't understand. A good dictionary and some patience help to keep up. This one, for example.

title: Dies
excerpt: The dies (Dies Natalis) is the birthday of a Dutch student association, study association or university.
example: The association turned fifty this year, so the dies was celebrated extra big.
text: Dies Natalis is Latin for birthday. The day is often celebrated with a borrel or party. When it is a big round anniversary it often turns into a lustrum, with a whole week of festivities.

title: Digital footprint
excerpt: Your digital footprint is the trail of information you leave online, like posts, comments and accounts.
example: "They really looked me up for that internship. Luckily I had just cleaned up my digital footprint."
text: Everything you do online leaves traces. Some disappear fast. Others can still be found years later, like old tweets or party photos. Employers look at it more and more.

title: Dispuut
excerpt: A dispuut is a close-knit group within a Dutch student association, often with members from several years.
example: For three years she has had dinner with her dispuut every Thursday, no matter who still has to study.
text: A dispuut works like its own little club with its own activities, traditions and often its own colours. Usually you get invited to join instead of signing up yourself. It is a bit like a sorority or fraternity chapter, but smaller.

title: Dissertation
excerpt: A dissertation is a big research project or paper you write as part of your degree.
example: "See you all after the summer. First I have to finish my dissertation."
text: In the UK a dissertation is usually the final paper of your bachelor or master. In the US it is the big PhD project. In the Netherlands it is called a scriptie, and most students just call it their thesis.

title: Dive bar
excerpt: A dive bar is a simple, cheap bar without any fuss.
example: "Forget the cocktail bar. We're going to that dive bar around the corner, beer is two euros there."
text: Dive bar sounds negative, but it is often said with love. It is about places that feel real and relaxed. Sticky floor, old jukebox and regulars at the bar. The Dutch version is the bruin café, the brown cafe. Students love them.

title: DM
excerpt: DM stands for direct message. A private message on Instagram, TikTok or another platform.
example: "I'll send you those photos by DM. Not in the group chat."
text: DM can be the message itself, but also the verb: to DM someone. It is used a lot for flirting. Sending someone an unexpected message is called sliding into their DMs.

title: Doomscrolling
excerpt: Doomscrolling means scrolling through your phone endlessly, often past bad news, while you actually want to stop.
example: "I wanted to sleep at eleven, but at two I was still doomscrolling."
text: The word got big during the pandemic, when everyone kept reading bad news. Now people use it for any pointless scrolling. It often leads to bad sleep and a serious dose of brainrot.

title: Doorhalen
excerpt: Doorhalen means going out all night until the next morning, without sleeping.
example: They decided to doorhalen and only cycle home when the sun came up.
text: People often keep drinking to fight the tiredness. The price comes the next day, usually as a massive hangover and a very brak Sunday. It is the party version of an all-nighter.

title: Dorm
excerpt: A dorm is a student residence or student room, especially at American universities.
example: "During my exchange in Boston I shared a dorm with a guy from Texas."
text: Dorm is short for dormitory. In the US you often live in a dorm on campus in your first year, usually with a roommate. In the UK it is called halls. In the Netherlands most students live in a studentenhuis, a shared student house in the city. In Belgium it is a kot.

title: Double texting
excerpt: Double texting means sending a second message while the other person hasn't replied to your first one yet.
example: "She hasn't replied yet. Can I double text or is that too much?"
text: In normal conversations double texting is totally fine. In dating it is sometimes seen as too eager. In the end it is mostly a feeling. An honest message beats waiting forever.

title: Down bad
excerpt: Being down bad means you are so desperately in love or lonely that it gets a little embarrassing.
example: "He drove three hours back and forth to return her charger. He's seriously down bad."
text: Originally down bad meant things were going badly for you, for example money-wise. Now it is mostly about love and longing. Everyone sees it, except the person who is down bad.

title: Dragged
excerpt: Getting dragged means being heavily criticised or laughed at, often by lots of people online at once.
example: "He posted his opinion on pineapple pizza and got dragged in the comments all day."
text: Getting dragged is about loud, public criticism. Usually after a controversial post or a clear blunder. It is a bit less serious than getting cancelled. Often it blows over after a few days.

title: Five-second rule
excerpt: The five-second rule says you can still eat food you dropped, as long as you pick it up within five seconds.
example: His fry fell on the floor, but he picked it up right away. Five-second rule.
text: Took longer than that? Then by the rules it goes in the bin. Not that anyone actually counts. Fun fact: the Dutch are stricter. They call it the driesecondenregel, the three-second rule.

title: Drinking game
excerpt: A drinking game is a game where you drink based on the rules, results or mistakes in the game.
example: "Anyone got an idea for a drinking game? We have cards and a few cups."
text: Famous drinking games are beer pong, Kings Cup and flip cup. The Dutch have their own classics too, like Kingsen and Bakplaten. Because you sometimes drink fast, it is smart to keep track of how much you actually had.

title: Drip
excerpt: Drip is a stylish outfit or good taste in clothes. Someone with drip looks sharp.
example: "Did you see his outfit at the gala? That drip was insane."
text: Drip comes from hip hop. The idea is that you are so cool your style is dripping off you. Expensive trainers, a nice jacket, good combinations. People with drip usually like to flex it too.

title: Droog staan
excerpt: Droog staan (standing dry) means not drinking for a night on purpose, for example because you have to drive.
example: Because he had to drive that night, he decided to droog staan at the borrel.
text: There is usually a practical reason to droog staan. Driving, work the next day or just a quiet night between parties without having to adten. At a Dutch student party you might need to explain it twice. But nobody really minds.

title: Dropout
excerpt: A dropout is someone who quits school or university before finishing.
example: "Mark Zuckerberg is a dropout too, so maybe I'll be fine."
text: People stop for all kinds of reasons, like money, health or a different plan. The word can be neutral, but it sometimes sounds like a judgement. In the Netherlands a negative BSA after your first year forces some students out.

title: Dry texting
excerpt: Dry texting is replying with very short, uninterested messages that make a conversation die.
example: "I ask how his weekend was and he just says 'fine'. What a dry texter."
text: One-word answers, no questions back and no emojis. It makes it look like someone isn't interested. Sometimes that is true. But some people just text short.

title: DTR
excerpt: DTR stands for define the relationship. The talk where you figure out what you two actually are.
example: "We've been dating for two months now. I think it's time for the DTR talk."
text: In a DTR talk you discuss whether you are exclusive and what you expect from each other. It often comes after a talking stage or a situationship. Scary, but it saves a lot of confusion.

title: Dubbel gemengd
excerpt: A dubbel gemengd (double mixed) student house has both men and women, from different student associations.
example: In their dubbel gemengd house, members of four different associations lived together.
text: Some Dutch student houses only mix on gender, or only on association. Dubbel gemengd mixes both. It is just one of the many types of houses you find in a Dutch student city. When you go house hunting, the ad usually says which type it is.

title: Duet
excerpt: A duet is a TikTok feature that puts your video side by side with someone else's.
example: "She made a duet with that singing video and sang the second voice. Now she's viral."
text: Duets are used for reactions, challenges, singing and jokes. The original video stays visible next to the new one. A stitch is similar, but there you put a clip of the original before your own video.

title: Duft
excerpt: Duft is the Dutch nickname for a student from Delft, also called a fietsenmaker (bike mechanic).
example: "Such a duft," they joked when he started talking about his engineering degree again.
text: Delft is home to the biggest technical university in the Netherlands. So its students get teased for being nerdy engineers. The nickname fietsenmaker is a wink to that technical image. Students in other cities say it with love. Mostly.

title: DUO
excerpt: DUO is the Dutch government agency that handles student finance and student loans.
example: Luckily the money from DUO was back in her account at the end of the month.
text: DUO stands for Dienst Uitvoering Onderwijs. Students lovingly call it "ome DUO", uncle DUO. For a lot of students it is their main source of income while studying. The monthly payment is called stufi. Internationals can sometimes apply too, depending on their situation.

title: EL CID
excerpt: EL CID is the introduction week for new students in Leiden.
example: During EL CID she met more students in one week than in all her years of secondary school.
text: The name stands for Eerste Leidse Commissie Introductie Dagen. You get to know the city, your studies and student life, usually with a small group of other first-years. Every Dutch city has its own version. It is the Dutch take on Freshers' Week.

title: Elective
excerpt: An elective is a course you choose yourself, instead of a required part of your programme.
example: "For my elective I'm doing wine tasting for beginners. I'm expecting a ten."
text: Electives let you explore another interest or specialise further. They also just earn you credits. At Dutch universities a bigger block of electives is called a minor.

title: Engagement bait
excerpt: Engagement bait is content made mainly to get likes, comments and shares, so more people see it.
example: "Tag someone who is always late!" Sure. Classic engagement bait.
text: Think of questions, controversial opinions or "tag a friend". The more interaction, the more the algorithm shows it. It gets annoying when the interaction matters more than the content. Rage bait and clickbait are family.

title: Era
excerpt: An era is a period or phase in your life, style or interests. Online, every phase gets called an era.
example: "I worked out three days in a row. I'm fully in my gym era."
text: The word got extra popular because of Taylor Swift and her Eras Tour. Now you put it behind anything: your study era, your single era or your chaotic era. That way a short phase becomes a whole chapter.
